Truly, tackling this topic requires a thorough treatment of the intricacies involved. Power law scaling in neural networks suggests that the complexity of the model grows exponentially with the size of the training dataset, which implies a significant increase in computational resources and data storage needs. However, this doesn't necessarily mean that an exponential increase in dataset size is required to achieve modest performance improvements.

Instead, the power law scaling phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that neural networks with more parameters tend to have a greater capacity to learn complex patterns in the data. This capacity is often measured by the number of parameters, which grows exponentially with the size of the training dataset. However, the relationship between dataset size and performance improvements is not always exponential.

In fact, research has shown that the relationship between dataset size and performance improvements can be more nuanced, with diminishing returns often observed at larger dataset sizes. This is because larger datasets can lead to overfitting, where the model becomes too specialized to the training data and fails to generalize well to new, unseen data.

Furthermore, the choice of optimization algorithm, hyperparameters, and model architecture can also significantly impact the performance of neural networks, even with large datasets. Therefore, it's not necessarily the case that an exponential increase in dataset size is required to achieve modest performance improvements.

In conclusion, while power law scaling in neural networks does suggest that the complexity of the model grows exponentially with the size of the training dataset, the relationship between dataset size and performance improvements is more complex and influenced by various factors.
